extracted.intended_audience: authors and statisticians conducting systematic reviews and meta-analyses (eg, Cochrane review authors)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for planning, conducting and interpreting meta-analyses and related analyses (subgroup analyses, meta-regression, handling missing data, Bayesian methods, and sensitivity analyses) within systematic reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confounding of study characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Two characteristics are confounded if their influences on the intervention effect cannot be disentangled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confounding complicates interpretation of subgroup analyses and meta-regressions and can lead to incorrect conclusions (example: intensive therapy coinciding with more severe patients). Compute correlations between study characteristics to identify possible confounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collinearity in meta-regression
rubrics_metrics.description: Co-linearity between potential effect modifiers in meta-regression impedes separating their individual influences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collinearity causes similar interpretive difficulties as confounding. Check for correlations among covariates before meta-regression; be cautious interpreting coefficients when predictors are correlated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subgroup comparisons are observational
rubrics_metrics.description: Subgroup analyses and meta-regressions investigate differences between studies and are observational in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remember that participants are not randomized to trials; subgroup findings are subject to biases of observational studies (eg, confounding). A subgroup difference does not prove causality for the defining subgroup characteristic (illustrated by sibling donor age example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-specified versus post-hoc subgroup analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should state whether subgroup analyses were pre-specified or undertaken post hoc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place more reliance on a small number of pre-specified subgroup analyses. Numerous post-hoc subgroup analyses are data dredging and increase risk of false findings. For continuous variables, ensure cut-points are chosen independently of observed differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for indirect/external evidence supporting subgroup findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences between subgroups should be clinically plausible and supported by other external or indirect evidence to be convincing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for corroborating evidence from other studies or mechanistic plausibility before inferring subgroup effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess practical importance of subgroup differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the magnitude of difference between subgroups would change recommendations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If subgroup differences are too small to affect decisions, it may be preferable to report overall results only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical test for differences between subgroups
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare magnitudes of effects across subgroups directly (eg, calculate a P value for the difference).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not infer subgroup differences by comparing statistical significance within subgroups; use formal tests of interaction or difference between subgroup estimates (see Section 10.11.3.1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Within-study versus between-study subgroup relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences observed within studies are more reliable than analyses of subsets of studies (between-study).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Within-study relationships replicated across multiple studies increase confidence. Prefer within-study comparisons where possible to reduce ecological bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a formal credibility instrument (ICEMAN)
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal assessment of subgroup/meta-regression credibility is facilitated by the ICEMAN checklist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply ICEMAN for meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials to cover considerations such as pre-specification, plausibility, magnitude, statistical strength, replication, and potential confounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigating effect by underlying risk (comparator group risk)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether variation in underlying average outcome risk across studies explains heterogeneity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparator group risk (CGR) is a summary of case-mix but is controversial because it conflates known and unknown factors and depends on follow-up length. Use caution interpreting relationships of effect estimates with CGR; consult Sharp (2001) and consider implications of choice of summary statistic (see Section 10.4.3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of summary statistic with respect to underlying risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Different summary statistics (risk ratio, odds ratio, risk difference) relate differently to underlying risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer summary statistics that show little relationship with underlying risk for meta-analysis. Consider how absolute and relative measures behave across different baseline risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regression to the mean when relating effect estimates to comparator risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Regression to the mean can create a false correlation between effect estimates and comparator group risks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A chance high comparator risk tends to produce higher-than-expected effect estimates and vice versa. Use methods that correct for regression to the mean (require sophisticated software) and seek statistical expertise (references McIntosh 1996, Thompson et al 1997).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dose–response (treatment intensity/duration) analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Meta-regression principles apply to dose-response, intensity or duration, but such conclusions are stronger when doses are randomized within studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious interpreting between-study dose-response relationships due to confounding and low power; avoid concluding absence of dose-response without considering limited power of meta-regression analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of missing data in systematic reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Missing data can occur as missing studies, missing outcomes, missing summary data, missing individuals in reported results, and missing study-level characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table 10.12.a lists possible reasons (eg, publication bias, selective reporting, incomplete reporting, attrition). Recognize all levels where data can be absent and where to look for more information (Chapters 4, 7, 8, 23).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not exclude studies solely for missing summary data
rubrics_metrics.description: Most methodologists believe missing summary data should not be a reason to exclude a study from a systematic review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include studies with missing summary data in the review and discuss implications for meta-analysis; consider imputation or approximations (eg, imputing SDs, correlation coefficients) where appropriate (see Chapters 6 and 23).

rubrics_metrics.name: MECIR C64: Addressing missing outcome data (expectation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider implications of missing participant-level outcome data; follow intention-to-treat principles where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incomplete outcome data can bias results. Use statistical analyses and careful interpretation; consider imputation methods accompanied by sensitivity analyses. Risk of bias due to incomplete outcome data should be assessed using Cochrane RoB tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think why data may be missing (MAR vs NMAR)
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate data missing at random (MAR) from not missing at random (NMAR) and consider consequences for bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If missingness is unrelated to true values (MAR), analyses of available data may be unbiased. If missingness depends on the unobserved values (NMAR), analyses of available data are likely biased. Publication bias, selective reporting, attrition often produce NMAR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principal options for handling missing data
rubrics_metrics.description: Main options: (1) analyse only available data; (2) impute missing values and treat them as observed; (3) impute and account for imputation uncertainty (eg, multiple imputation); (4) use statistical models making assumptions about missingness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Option 2 (single imputation) is practical but understates uncertainty. Options 3 and 4 require statistical expertise. Choose methods appropriate to the plausibility of assumptions and report them transparently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five general recommendations for missing data handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommended steps: contact original investigators; make assumptions explicit; follow Chapter 8 for RoB assessment; perform sensitivity analyses; address implications in Discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document assumptions (eg, MAR, worst outcome), seek additional data when feasible, and use sensitivity analyses to explore how conclusions change under alternative assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods for missing outcome data from individual participants
rubrics_metrics.description: Use sensitivity analyses based on plausible assumptions about how missing participants' risks differ from observed participants; specific strategies exist for dichotomous and continuous outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higgins et al propose strategies for dichotomous outcomes using different assumptions about event risk among missing participants; Akl et al propose simple imputation suites. Apply analogous methods for continuous data (Ebrahim et al). Avoid double counting events and be cautious about worst/best case analyses which may not reflect plausible scenarios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bayesian meta-analysis principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Bayesian analysis combines a prior distribution and likelihood to produce a posterior; results typically reported as point estimate and 95% credible interval interpreted as probability statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bayesian interpretations differ from classical inference; probabilities depend on the prior. Perform sensitivity analyses to priors. Use software such as WinBUGS, R implementations, or meta-regression tricks; seek statistical expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantages of Bayesian approaches for meta-analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Potential advantages include incorporation of external evidence, decision-making extensions (utilities), accommodating imprecision in between-study variance, investigating relationships with underlying risk, enabling complex analyses (eg, network meta-analysis), and quantifying how data change beliefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These advantages make Bayesian methods attractive especially when few studies exist; use data-based prior libraries for heterogeneity where appropriate (eg, Turner et al 2012).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation for statistical expertise and use of priors
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistical expertise is strongly recommended for Bayesian analyses; most analysts use non-informative priors for intervention effects but may use informative/data-based priors for between-study heterogeneity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that different priors can yield different results; carry out sensitivity analyses. Consult texts and resources (Sutton et al, Spiegelhalter et al) and consider libraries of priors derived from many meta-analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and definition of sensitivity analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: A sensitivity analysis repeats the primary analysis substituting alternative decisions or values for arbitrary or unclear choices to assess robustness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sensitivity analyses to ask whether findings are robust to eligibility decisions, analytic choices, missing data assumptions, and other arbitrary choices. Pre-specify some sensitivity analyses when possible; others may emerge during review.

rubrics_metrics.name: MECIR C71: Expectation to use sensitivity analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Use sensitivity analyses to assess robustness of results to notable assumptions, imputed data, borderline decisions and studies at high risk of bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifying when results are robust strengthens conclusions; where sensitivity analyses show influential uncertainties, seek further data or interpret results with caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision nodes and examples for sensitivity analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Many points may generate sensitivity analyses: study searching, eligibility criteria (participants, intervention, comparator, outcome, study design), which data to analyse, and analysis methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: whether to include abstracts; age cut-offs; dose ranges; comparator definitions; time points; blinded vs unblinded assessments; whether to use change scores vs post-intervention values; how to impute missing SDs; ICC values for cluster trials; within-subject correlations for crossover trials; assumptions about missing outcomes; fixed vs random-effects; choice of effect measure (OR, RR, RD) or use of SMD vs mean differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish sensitivity analyses from subgroup analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensitivity analyses and subgroup analyses differ in aim and interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sensitivity analyses test robustness of results to analytic choices and do not attempt to estimate effects in excluded subsets. Subgroup analyses estimate effects within defined groups and make formal statistical comparisons across subgroups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting sensitivity analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Report sensitivity analyses clearly, preferably in a summary table.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A summary table is usually most informative; rarely is it useful to present many separate forest plots for each sensitivity analysis.
